# Sources: "What if the Moon disappeared?" (topic discovery)

Access counts: read = S1, S2, S3, S4, S5. Everything else was seen only as a search summary (snippet): a lead, never
evidence. Nothing in subject.json or claims.json rests on a snippet alone.

### S1. NOAA National Ocean Service, "What Causes Tides" (Tides and Water Levels tutorial), NOAA Ocean Service Education, undated
- Secondary: a federal agency's educational explainer (NOAA's National Ocean Service, the US authority on tides), not a study. URL: https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/education/tutorial_tides/tides02_cause.html
- Access: read (the page text on the Sun's and Moon's tide-generating forces, with its figure captions)
- Supports: C01 (the Sun's tide-generating force "is about half that of the moon"; the Sun has 27 million times the Moon's mass but is 390 times farther away). Counterevidence: none; S2 says "a little less than half", which agrees. The page does not cover tides from the Sun alone, spring and neap tides, or their timing.
- Status: credible secondary, no revision date shown. The cube of the distance shows up garbled as "3903" (390 cubed) in the page text. Independent of S2, and the two agree.

### S2. NASA Science (written by Tracy Vogel; science advisors Vishnu Viswanathan, Joseph Renaud; NASA Goddard), "Tides", science.nasa.gov, last updated 12 February 2026
- Secondary: an agency explainer checked by NASA scientists. URL: https://science.nasa.gov/moon/tides
- Access: read (the explainer text as fetched)
- Supports: C01 (the Sun has "a little less than half of the Moon's tide-generating force"), C02 (spring tides at full and new Moon when Earth, Sun and Moon line up; neap tides around the first and last quarter), C03 (a point on Earth needs about 50 extra minutes to turn back under the Moon). Counterevidence: none. It does not cover the slowing of Earth's spin, the Moon's retreat or a world without the Moon.
- Status: credible secondary and current (2026). Independent of S1.

### S3. Kronfeld-Schor N., Dominoni D., de la Iglesia H., Levy O., Herzog E.D., Dayan T., Helfrich-Forster C., "Chronobiology by moonlight", Proceedings of the Royal Society B 280: 20123088, published 22 August 2013
- Secondary: a peer-reviewed review by specialists in animal timing, ecology and coral biology. URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3712431/ (DOI 10.1098/rspb.2012.3088)
- Access: read (the main text up to the reference list; the reference list was cut off). The primary studies it cites were not read: they are indirect.
- Supports: C04 (corals spawning together several nights after the full Moon), C05 (Pocillopora damicornis releasing larvae out of synchrony under constant full-moon or constant new-moon conditions), C06 (coral cry2 expressed more on full-moon nights, "suggesting" a role), C07 (Clunio marinus: moonlight in southern populations, water turbulence in northern ones), C08 (eagle owls, coyotes, migrating land birds), C09 (the mechanisms are "even less understood"). Counterevidence: the review says itself that the mechanisms are poorly understood, that lab results (fruit flies) may differ from the field, and that moonlight's part is hard to separate from other cues. Most examples rest on a single study.
- Status: credible review from 2013. Later work may refine single cases; nothing found that replaces it. Its examples of lions attacking people, blood-feeding bats, snakes at carrion and stress hormones measured in faeces are left out under the content rules.

### S4. Laskar J., Joutel F., Robutel P. (Bureau des Longitudes, Paris), "Stabilization of the Earth's obliquity by the Moon", Nature 361: 615-617, 18 February 1993
- Primary: the study itself, peer-reviewed (Earth's precession integrated over 18 million years for every starting tilt). URL: https://perso.imcce.fr/jacques-laskar/pdf/Laskar_Joutel_Robutel_1993.pdf (DOI 10.1038/361615a0)
- Access: read (the whole paper. The PDF is a scan the fetcher could not read as text, so its three pages were taken out as images and read one by one: summary, text, captions of Figs. 1-4, Box 2, conclusion.)
- Supports: C10 (geological records give a spin about 1.22 times today's 2.5 billion years ago, slowed since by tidal dissipation), C11 (with the Moon the tilt is "essentially stable"; without it "the chaotic zone would then extend from nearly 0 deg up to about 85 deg"), C12 (variations of 1.3 deg either side of 23.3 deg), C13 (Moon removed and present parameters kept: "from 15 deg to 32 deg in 1 Myr"), C14 (one side: more than 50 deg in a few million years and more than 85 deg in the long term, "for many values of the Earth primordial spin rate"; Figs. 3-4 are computed at 1.22 and 1.6 times today's spin), C15 (Milankovitch: ice ages linked to changes in sunlight caused by orbit and orientation, tilt included), C17 (tidal dissipation will in the end drive Earth into the large chaotic zone). Counterevidence: later studies (S5, S6) find a moonless Earth's tilt drifts much more slowly, or within narrower limits. The paper's own climate wording is hedged ("might have driven", "would probably have").
- Status: primary record from 1993, widely cited. Later work revises its long-run range. Its main qualitative finding, that the Moon steadies the tilt, is repeated by S5. Important for this video: the famous "0 to 85 degrees" belongs to faster early spins and the long term. For today's Earth with the Moon removed, the paper reports 15 to 32 degrees within a million years.

### S5. Li G., Batygin K., "On the spin-axis dynamics of a Moonless Earth", The Astrophysical Journal 790: 69 (2014); arXiv:1404.7505, submitted 29 April 2014
- Primary: the study itself (analytical estimates of how fast the tilt drifts in a chaotic regime, compared with published numerical runs). URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/1404.7505 (DOI 10.1088/0004-637X/790/1/69)
- Access: read (abstract only)
- Supports: C11 ("the Earth's obliquity is stabilized by the Moon, and would undergo chaotic variations in the Moon's absence"), C14 (the other side: the random change in tilt is "sufficiently slow to not preclude long-term habitability"). Counterevidence: the larger, faster long-run ranges in S4. The abstract gives no numbers, and the full text was not read.
- Status: primary, 2014, independent of S4. Newer than S4 and, by its own account, consistent with published numerical experiments.

### S6. Lissauer J.J., Barnes J.W., Chambers J.E., "Obliquity variations of a moonless Earth", Icarus 217: 77-87, 2012
- Primary: the study itself (a moonless Earth's tilt integrated directly for up to 4 billion years). URL: https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012Icar..217...77L/abstract
- Access: snippet (search summaries of the abstract from a third-party index. The ADS page came back empty and the index page reset the connection, so nothing was read.)
- Supports: nothing rests on it. C14 names it as "reported to find" a much narrower range over billions of years, steadier tilts for backward (retrograde) spin, and smaller ranges for days shorter than 12 hours. Counterevidence: S4.
- Status: not verified here. Read the abstract before the script uses any of its numbers.

### S7. Lissauer J.J. et al. (attribution unchecked), NASA Technical Reports Server record 20040068133, 2004
- Primary (a conference abstract, if the search summary is right). URL: https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20040068133
- Access: snippet (a search summary said it reports a moonless Earth's tilt staying within roughly 12 to 38 degrees over 100 million years)
- Supports: nothing. A lead that roughly agrees with C13. Counterevidence: none seen.
- Status: not verified, including who wrote it.

### S8. Popular Science, "What would happen if the moon suddenly disappeared?" (quoting planetary scientist Matthew Siegler), date not seen
- Popular: a magazine explainer quoting a planetary scientist. URL: https://www.popsci.com/what-would-happen-if-moon-suddenly-disappeared
- Access: snippet (search summary only)
- Supports: C16 (legend: the tilt going from "no tilt" to "a drastic tilt" with ice ages "in just a few hundred thousand years"). It also gives tides at "about one third" of today's swing, which matches the reasoned M3 but is not relied on. Counterevidence: S4's calculation for today's spin (15-32 deg in a million years) and S5's slow drift.
- Status: popular and unverified. Used only to see how the question is usually answered.

### S9. Astronomy.com, "What if the Moon disappeared tomorrow?", date not seen
- Popular: a magazine Q&A. URL: https://www.astronomy.com/science/what-if-the-moon-disappeared-tomorrow/
- Access: snippet
- Supports: nothing. Background only: tides "under half"; the tilt change gradual, not noticed "within our lifetime".
- Status: popular, unverified.

### S10. ZME Science, "What would happen if the Moon actually disappeared?", date not seen
- Popular. URL: https://www.zmescience.com/space/what-would-happen-if-the-moon-actually-disappeared
- Access: snippet
- Supports: nothing. Background only: tides "50% to 75% lower"; a wobble of "10 to 45 degrees", which disagrees with S8.
- Status: popular, unverified. Shows that the popular figures disagree with each other.

### S11. NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory, "The Apollo experiment that keeps on giving" (news article), date not seen
- Secondary: an agency news article on lunar laser ranging. URL: https://jpl.nasa.gov/news/the-apollo-experiment-that-keeps-on-giving/
- Access: snippet
- Supports: nothing. A lead for alternative T4: the Moon moving away about 3.8 cm a year, measured by laser ranging to the reflectors left by Apollo. Another JPL page, also seen only as a snippet, gives 3.7 cm.
- Status: not verified here.

### S12. Authors not seen, "On the Relation of the Lunar Recession and the Length-of-the-Day", arXiv:2110.09037, 2021
- Primary (preprint). URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2110.09037
- Access: snippet
- Supports: nothing. A lead: a fit of 38.30 +/- 0.09 mm a year from ranges taken 1970-2015, with the Moon's retreat tied to the lengthening day.
- Status: preprint, not verified here.

### S13. Dacke M. et al., "Insect orientation to polarized moonlight", Nature 424: 33, 2003
- Primary. URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/424033a
- Access: snippet (through search summaries of National Geographic, Discover and Lund University coverage)
- Supports: nothing yet. A strong lead for the night beat: an African dung beetle keeps a straight course by polarised moonlight and wanders on moonless or cloudy nights; a later study (not seen) found the Milky Way as a weaker backup.
- Status: not verified here. Read it before any use.

### S14. NOAA National Ocean Service, "Tides06 variations" (tutorial page), undated
- Secondary. URL: https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/education/tutorial_tides/tides06_variations.html
- Access: snippet
- Supports: C02, only as an unread second source that agrees (spring tides at new and full Moon, neap tides at the quarters).
- Status: not verified here.
